## 1. Intro and framework

- Evan has conducted thousands of interviews
- Framework: requirements → core entities → API → (no data flow; product-style question) → HLD → deep dives
  - HLD meets functional requirements only; deep dives meet the NFRs

## 2. Functional requirements

- Unknown system? Ask lots of questions; here everyone knows LeetCode
- Phrase as "users should be able to…" (prefix can be skipped to save typing)
1. **View a list of problems**
2. **View a problem and code a solution**
3. **Submit a solution and get feedback** (passed all tests or not)
4. **Competitions with a live leaderboard**
   - Everyone starts together, solves a set of questions fast; leaderboard shows who leads

## 3. Non-functional requirements and scale

- Candidates: CAP, environment constraints, scalability, latency, durability, security, fault tolerance, compliance
  - Better framing: what makes this system uniquely challenging?
- **Availability over consistency**
  - A stale problem edit for a few seconds, or a leaderboard lagging a second, is fine
- **Security and isolation when running user code** (unique to this question)
- **Scale: competitions up to 100,000 users**
- **Fresh, near-real-time leaderboard**, ideally without page refresh
- Write-up adds: return submission results within ~5 s (write-up)
- Estimations: defer until a decision needs them; tell the interviewer
- But ask about scale
  - **100K DAU** (peak = a competition)
  - **~3,000 problems** (LeetCode had ~3,200 at recording)
- Stay focused on these requirements for the rest of the interview

## 4. Core entities

- Don't write the full data model yet; you may not know it; fill it in during the HLD
- **User**, **Problem**, **Submission**, **Competition**
- **Leaderboard**: hand-wavy; could just be an aggregation over submissions
- Tell the interviewer you'll detail schemas later ("99 out of 100 times" they agree)

## 5. API

- One endpoint per functional requirement, usually (sometimes 1:2)

```
GET  /problems?category&difficulty&page&pageSize  -> Partial<Problem>[]
GET  /problems/:problemId                          -> Problem
POST /problems/:problemId/submit                   -> Submission
     body: { code, language, competitionId? }
GET  /leaderboard/:competitionId?page&pageSize     -> Leaderboard
```

- List returns **partial problems** (id, name, difficulty, category): problems are big (tests, stubs); smaller payload is faster
- Query params for optional things; path params for required ones
- POST creates a submission row
  - Resource naming/verbs: interviewers rarely care ("I've read your comments")
- Large code could go to S3 first with a URL in the body; here solutions are capped at tens of KB, so inline is fine
- Leaderboard paginated: up to 100K participants (page-based; cursor is the alternative)

## 6. HLD: list and view problems

- Stay linear through the requirements; avoid distractions
  - Common pitfall: inventing features (Yelp review replies, admin emails) not agreed upfront
  - Interviews last 35–50 minutes
- No microservices here: requirements are simple; **client, primary server, database**
- Problem: id, name, difficulty, category (+ later: code stubs per language, test cases, description)
- List: query with filters (WHERE clauses) and pagination
- DB choice doesn't matter: 100K DAU, few writes; Postgres or DynamoDB; don't overthink it
- View: query by primary key (problem id)
- Coding happens client-side in an embedded editor like **Monaco** (open source)

## 7. HLD: submit and run code (isolation options)

- **Bad: run user code on the API server**
  - Malicious code could crash the server, delete data, DDoS, mine crypto
  - Untrusted code must be **isolated**
  - Normally HLD stays simple, but this is too dangerous to leave; fix it now (or at least flag it)
- **VM** on the server
  - Fully isolated; crashes and malice stay inside
  - Runs a full OS: resource-heavy, slow to start, needs more hardware
- **Container** (Docker)
  - Shares the host OS; packages only code + dependencies
  - Lighter, efficient; more instances per machine; cheaper
  - One container image per runtime (Java, Python, …) with dependencies installed
- **Serverless functions** (AWS Lambda)
  - Small, stateless, event-driven; cloud provider scales them
  - Problem: **cold starts** (spin up, load dependencies); warming them ≈ having containers
- Evan picks **containers** on a set of servers
  - Primary server sends code; container runs tests; returns pass/fail, errors, runtime
  - Primary server saves a **Submission**: passed (bool), errors, runtime, test results

## 8. HLD: competitions and leaderboard

- Define "competition" with the interviewer (ideally earlier)
  - Starts at a set time, lasts **90 minutes**, **10 problems**
  - Up to **100K users**
  - Winner: most problems solved; tie-break by fastest
- Competition: id, startTime, endTime, problemIds
- Submission adds: competitionId, problemId, userId, submittedAt
- Simple leaderboard: query submissions for the competition, group by user, count passed, tie-break by time

```sql
SELECT userId, COUNT(*) AS solved, MIN(submittedAt) AS t
FROM submissions
WHERE competitionId = ? AND passed = true
GROUP BY userId
ORDER BY solved DESC, t ASC;
```

- Written fast, "may or may not be perfect"; you'd explain it, not write it
- Call out it's expensive under heavy reads; fix in deep dives

## 9. Deep dive: security and isolation

- Containers already separate code from the server, DB, file system
- **Infinite loops**: explicit **timeout** per execution (e.g., 5 s); kill and return an error
- **Fork bombs / memory / CPU abuse**: **CPU and memory limits** per container; exceed and it's torn down
  - Don't reveal exact limits in errors, so users can't reverse-engineer them
- Also
  - **Read-only file system**; write only to a temp dir
  - **Network isolation** (VPC controls in AWS)
  - **No system calls** on the box
- Write-up names: seccomp for syscalls; VPC security groups and NACLs (write-up)
- Write-up: saying "Docker with limited network, CPU/memory bounds, and a timeout" is likely sufficient (write-up)

## 10. Deep dive: fast, fresh leaderboard

- Two problems: the query is slow and costly; users want updates without refreshing
  - 100K entries × a few hundred bytes; DynamoDB cost estimate "on the order of $50 per query" (see the site's DynamoDB write-up)
- **Cache with TTL** (Redis, ~10 s)
  - Run the query on a miss, cache it
  - Unlucky users at each expiry pay the slow query
- **Cron job refreshes the cache** every ~10 s (no TTL)
  - Value: key `leaderboard:<competitionId>` → JSON of ranked users and scores
  - All reads hit the cache
  - Stale up to the interval; shorter intervals can overlap if the query takes longer than the interval
  - Extra dependency: if the cron breaks, the cache stalls or a thundering herd hits the DB
  - Fine for mid-level; not terrible at senior; not the best
- **Update the cached JSON on each write**
  - Read the big blob, parse, update one user, save
  - Redis is single-threaded, so races are OK; but reading a 100K-entry blob each time is heavy
- **Redis sorted set** (the pick)
  - Sorted set = unique elements, each with a score that orders them
  - Efficient range queries by score or rank: page 2 = ranks 100–200; O(log n), in memory
  - Element = userId; score = solved count, with decimals for the time tie-break
  - On submission: write DB, then update the user's score
  - Write-up commands: `ZADD competition:leaderboard:{id} {score} {userId}`; `ZRANGE … 0 N-1 REV WITHSCORES` (write-up)
  - Write-up: `ZREVRANGE` deprecated since Redis 6.2 (write-up)
- **Near real time**: agree with the interviewer on ~2–5 s
  - **Poll every ~3 s** for the current page
  - Candidates always want WebSockets/SSE; raise it, but it's over-engineering here
    - Extra infrastructure, a connection manager, stateful servers (hurts fault tolerance)
    - Not worth a couple of seconds of freshness
  - Write-up: progressive polling, every 2 s near the end, 10 s otherwise (write-up)
  - Write-up: staff candidates know the complex solution and say why it's overkill (write-up)
- **DB and cache consistency**: server could crash between the two writes
  - **CDC**: DynamoDB Streams / Postgres logical replication → queue (Kafka) → worker updates Redis
  - If Redis dies: replay the stream, or more likely reload from the DB

## 11. Deep dive: scale for 100K-user competitions

- Availability: already favored (no ACID transactions or locking); LBs, horizontal scale go without saying (except maybe mid-level)
- Risk: dropping submissions in the end-of-competition surge
- **Pre-scaling**: provision many containers beforehand; expensive, and you may guess wrong
- **Dynamic scaling**: autoscale on CPU/memory (e.g., ECS on Fargate)
  - Probably not fast enough for a sudden 100K-submission spike
- **Queue as a buffer** (the pick)
  - Submission → message queue (Kafka or SQS; choice not important)
  - Workers pull, run code in containers, report back; primary server writes DB; CDC updates cache
  - Workers and containers scale; retries possible
- Submissions are now async: how does the user get the result?
  - Holding a REST request ~10 s is too long
  - **Poll** a check endpoint, e.g., `GET /problems/:id/submission/:submissionId`, for up to ~5 s
  - LeetCode itself polls a `/check` endpoint every ~3 s (visible in Chrome's Network tab)
- If code is large, store it in S3 and put only a reference on the queue
- Write-up's labels: vertical scaling (bad); dynamic horizontal scaling (great); horizontal scaling with queue (great) (write-up)

## 12. Deep dive: running test cases (write-up)

- Follow-up: "How would you actually run tests against code in any language?" (write-up)
  - Breaks candidates out of "box drawing mode"
- One test set per problem, not per language (write-up)
- Standard serialization for inputs/outputs + a test harness per language (write-up)
  - E.g., trees serialized as level-order (BFS) arrays: `[3,9,20,null,null,15,7]` → 3
  - Each language's `TreeNode` deserializes and compares to expected output

## 13. What is expected at each level

- Evan mostly asks this of mid-level and senior; "on the easier side" for staff (though some big tech companies ask staff)
- **Mid-level**
  - Realize code isolation matters; Docker or Lambda is a great first step
  - A timeout is the key extra
  - See the leaderboard query is slow; cache + cron refresh would pass
  - Brainstorm handling the end-of-competition surge (pre-scale, autoscale, queue)
  - Write-up: clear API and data model; working HLD; container, VM, or serverless (write-up)
- **Senior**
  - Land near the queue, or justify Lambda with pre-warming against cold starts
  - At least the cron cache; sorted set is great but variants work
  - One or two more security measures (CPU/memory bounds)
  - Write-up: container vs VM vs serverless trade-offs; how test cases actually run (write-up)
- Doing all of this at either level is "likely a hire"

## 14. Board as text (assembled from the talk)

```
Client (Monaco) -> Primary Server -> DB (Problem, Submission, Competition)
   ^ poll /check           |               | CDC (streams -> Kafka -> worker)
   ^ poll leaderboard      v               v
                     Submission Queue     Redis sorted set (leaderboard)
                           |
                        Workers -> Code containers per runtime
                                   (timeout, CPU/mem limits, read-only FS,
                                    no network, no syscalls)
```
